newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Moslem leader urges official recognition.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Moslem leader urges official recognition.

text.p: One of Bulgaria's rival Moslem leaders urged the country's new reformist government on Wednesday to reverse a decision of the former Socialist rulers and register his religious council.
The Supreme Court in March overturned a decision by the former Socialist cabinet to refuse to register Fikri Sali's High Moslem Council as Bulgaria's highest Moslem body.

"We await the speedy decision of the new government to mend the rough interference of the former ex-communist authorities and legalise us, because the patience of Bulgaria's Moslems has expired," Sali told a news conference.
He noted that parliament's Religious Creeds and Human Rights Commission had backed his appeal for recognition and advised the cabinet to legalise his council.
Sali appealed in 1995 to the Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg over the issue and a ruling is due in September.

"We will lauch a mass campaign for recognition and if we are not registered we will appeal to the Organisation of the Islamic Conference not to remove Bulgaria from its list of countries which do not respect Moslems' rights," he said.
Sali was chief mufti from 1992 to November 1994, when a national council elected Nedim Gendjev as head of the High Spiritual Council and appointed a new chief mufti.

In March 1995, more than 1,000 Moslems voted at a special national conference to restore Sali following allegations that Gendjev had once been an agent of the political department of the communist secret services.
Calling themselves the High Moslem Council, they sought registration from the Socialist government, which refused on the grounds that it had already registered a Moslem council.

Gendjev was appointed chief mufti in 1988, a year before communist ruler Todor Zhivkov was toppled. During the 1980s, one million ethnic Turks were forced to adopt Bulgarian names and their religious and human rights were severely curbed.
Their religious and cultural rights were restored after Zhivkov's overthrow and many of those who left for Turkey have since returned.
Bulgaria's President Petar Stoyanov is seeking Turkish support to remove Bulgaria from the OIC list of countries which do not respect Moslems' rights.

The dispute between Bulgaria's two Moslem authorities mirrors a longstanding row between the country's Orthodox Christians. The Supreme Court on March 5 declared invalid the registration of one of two rival synods of the Orthodox church.
